items.title: Xinhua Asia-Pacific news summary at 1600 GMT, Nov. 3
text: DHAKA -- Bangladesh and South Korea have agreed to establish a government-private sector working group to identify priority areas for cooperation and facilitate business engagement.

The understanding was reached at a bilateral meeting between Bangladeshi Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury and South Korean Trade Minister Park Jung-sung in Seoul on Monday, according to a statement from the Bangladeshi Finance Ministry on Tuesday. (Bangladesh-South Korea-Cooperation)

TOKYO -- Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi on Tuesday again called for discussions on reviewing the country's Three Non-Nuclear Principles and expressed support for considering the introduction of nuclear-powered submarines, Kyodo News reported.

Speaking at a seminar in Tokyo, Koizumi said an environment should be created in which necessary security policies can be discussed openly and frankly without prejudice. He added that, as Japan revises its three key security documents, society as a whole should develop a shared understanding of nuclear threats, according to the report. (Japan-Nuclear-Revision)
JAKARTA -- Indonesian police announced Tuesday evening that they have named three suspects in a case involving the alleged illegal wiretapping of several people, including President Prabowo Subianto.

Asep Safrudin, head of the Criminal Investigation Agency of the Indonesian National Police, told a press conference in Jakarta that the alleged wiretapping took place between 2025 and 2026. (Indonesia-Tapping-Suspect)

HONG KONG -- Hong Kong's real gross domestic product (GDP) expanded 5.2 percent year on year in the third quarter (Q3) of 2026, according to advance estimates released by the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) government on Tuesday.

US voters bring everyday worries to ballot box
text:
By LIA ZHU in San Francisco | 
          chinadaily.com.cn |
          Updated: 2026-11-04 12:48
When Rafael Martinez cast his ballot in New York, his concerns were close to home: the cost of living, healthcare and getting his family through rising prices.
"Honestly, it's been just about affordability and just getting my family through all these things," said Martinez, 43, of the Bronx.

As voters cast ballots in Tuesday's midterm elections, those interviewed by China Daily in New York and the San Francisco Bay Area spoke about prices they wanted brought down, services they wanted improved and a government they wanted to pay more attention to their lives.
For Maryanne Robinson, 60, a Bay Area resident, cheaper gasoline alone would not be enough.
"I think we need to see, not just the price of gas come down, but the price of goods as well," she said.

The interviews reflected individual views in the two regions, with criticism of the administration running through the conversations. Their concerns about household expenses echoed a national KFF poll conducted Sept 16-21.

The poll found six in 10 registered voters worried about affording healthcare, similar shares worried about gasoline and other transportation costs, and 52 percent expressed concern about affording food.
In Washington state, Torrance, who gave only his first name, told China Daily a few days ahead of Tuesday's elections that it cost him considerably more to fill a small car's gas tank now.
"My little Honda that I used to drive used to be only 40 bucks to fill up, now it's like 60 to 80," he said.
He blamed the Iran war and wanted greater attention paid to domestic problems than international affairs.
Robinson, a Canadian American, also criticized tariffs, particularly those on Canadian goods. "I'm really not happy about the tariffs," she said, "so I'd like to see that turned around as well."

Fellow Bay Area resident Rick Schaefer, 72, put healthcare first when asked about his biggest concern. He votes every year, he said, and regarded this election as particularly significant because it could change the balance of power in Washington.

Martinez also spoke about healthcare and its effects on communities. Asked about the government's performance, he said he felt its attention was directed toward corporate interests and affairs elsewhere rather than people at home.
He hoped the election would bring a less chaotic political environment.
"You just want to see some normalcy in politics again," he said.
For Gordon Curtis, 76, the concerns he brought to the election were less about what he could afford. To him, addressing issues in the judicial system and governing processes is more urgent.

Curtis grew up in Southern California and has lived in New York City since 1979. Its diversity was the primary reason he moved there, he said, describing his affection for people coming from other countries to live together.

"We are a nation of immigrants," he said. "I can cope with the rises in prices and all that. That matters to me less than the integrity of our judicial system, our governing processes which are being trampled underfoot."

items.title: Adidas bullish on growth opportunities in China
text:
By WANG YING in Shanghai | 
          China Daily |
          Updated: 2026-11-04 09:26
German sportswear company Adidas continues to explore opportunities in China and remains optimistic about the country's ambition to become a sports powerhouse, said a senior company executive.

"We believe strongly in the Chinese market, and we feel that there is plenty of energy in the economy compared with the stagnation we see in Europe," said Bjoern Gulden, CEO of Adidas, during a recent interview.

"The time when we were designing collections only in Germany or the United States is over. We are now designing all over the world and, believe it or not, the creative direction that is coming out of China and especially out of Shanghai is starting to play a more important role because the consumer wants it," said Gulden.

Adrian Siu, managing director of Adidas in China, said: "Currently, as much as 65 percent of products in the China market are designed by Adidas' Creation Center Shanghai. Among the products designed by the Creation Center Shanghai, 25 percent are already sold overseas and are very popular."

Driven by both sports and sports fashion, Adidas views a country's growing strength in part through improvements in its sporting achievements. At the same time, a country's rising influence in global fashion reflects its growing strength and cultural creativity, Siu said.

"Along with designing in Shanghai, manufacturing in China is making an impact globally and the company expects to keep contributing to the development of China's sports and fashion industries," Siu said.

Attending the recent 38th International Business Leaders' Advisory Council for the Mayor of Shanghai (IBLAC), Adidas submitted recommendations on how Shanghai can become a leading emotional vitality city at this year's meeting, which was focused on promoting innovation in Shanghai's service sector.

In its proposal, Adidas called for a new model of urban development that converts positive emotions into consumption growth, community vitality, cultural confidence and sustainable competitiveness. In the future, the cities that lead the world will be those that can create emotional resonance, and the company believes emotional vitality is becoming a new source of urban competitiveness, it explained.

The proposal noted that Shanghai's per capita spending on sporting goods rose from 922 yuan ($138) in 2008 to nearly 4,500 yuan in 2024. The city's sports economy has evolved from material consumption to experiential participation, and now toward emotional fulfillment.

Regarding China's goals for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period, Gulden said Adidas sees itself as a contributor to these goals, which also present significant opportunities for the sports industry and related businesses.

"The plan is great. I think there's a commitment to sports everywhere in China and we will of course support it because it's in our interest and sports is fun and the more people do it, the happier we will become," said Gulden.

items.title: Course charted for strict Party self-governance
text: As China enters a critical period in its modernization drive, the governing Communist Party of China has charted the course for tougher action against corruption and stronger self-governance in the years ahead.

Last week, the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee adopted a resolution on persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance, underscoring the need to step up the fight against corruption and strengthen checks on and oversight of the exercise of power.
In doing so, the CPC — the largest political party in the world, with more than 100 million members — is seeking to overcome the unique challenges facing a party of its size.

These challenges, as outlined by Xi Jinping, general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, include how to maintain the Party's strong governance and leadership capacity, and sustain a clean and upright political environment.

"It is now both imperative and timely for the Party to study issues concerning persevering with full and rigorous self-governance," Xi said in a January meeting of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee that set the agenda for the plenum.
At the January meeting, Xi said the decision to focus the plenary session on Party self-governance had been made after thorough deliberation.

Since it was founded in 1921, the Party has attached great importance to its self-supervision and self-governance. Today, the CPC's membership and ranks of officials have undergone structural changes, presenting new challenges for Party building.

In response to these challenges, Xi has repeatedly stressed the need for an unwavering commitment to strict Party self-governance, sending a clear signal that discipline will be enforced ever more strictly.
"It was with this in mind that the CPC Central Committee decided to make persevering with full and rigorous self-governance the plenum's agenda," he noted.

Explaining the resolution at the plenary session, Xi emphasized that persevering with full and rigorous self-governance is essential for maintaining the Party's advanced nature and integrity and consolidating its long-term governing position.
This year marks the beginning of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period, a critical time for achieving the goal of basically realizing socialist modernization by 2035.

"To successfully achieve the goals and tasks of the 15th Five-Year Plan, it is imperative to focus on enhancing the ability and competence of the Party in leading economic and social development," Xi told senior provincial — and ministerial-level officials attending a study session at the Party School of the CPC Central Committee earlier this year.
In January 2026, a drafting group was set up to prepare the resolution, with Xi at its helm.
Throughout the drafting process, he played a decisive role, chairing multiple meetings, delivering important speeches and issuing instructions to guide the work.
On Feb 6, Xi chaired the group's first plenary meeting, during which he outlined the key principles for the drafting of the resolution.

items.title: Rules of coexistence between man and machine
text: Robots, now numbering millions across factories and homes, serve as both solutions and challenges. They address issues such as economic productivity and care for an aging population, but also raise many questions that extend beyond technology into social and political realms.

For centuries, humans have used machines to replace physical labor. Machinery in textile mills sparked the industrial revolution and was followed by trains, cars and cranes that brought unprecedented progress and prosperity. The more than 4 million robots now working in industry worldwide continue that story, particularly aiding countries facing labor shortages and population declines.

However, we are a long way from a fully automated world. The Republic of Korea, which has one of the world's lowest birthrates and leads in automation, employs only one robot for every 10 manufacturing workers, while the global average is about one for every 70.

In domestic settings, the gap between science fiction and reality is even wider. While millions of robots now vacuum floors and mow lawns, the promise of automated homes has not materialized, partly because progress in dexterity has been slower than expected. We still lack robots capable of handling the complex needs of the elderly. Although some robots provide companionship, emotional support and basic physical assistance, the complexities of real home environments present significant challenges.

Since the 1960s, futurists have repeatedly warned that robots would destroy jobs on an epic scale, leading to mass unemployment. Most of these forecasts proved dramatically wrong: overall employment went up, not down, and more recent predictions, such as the disappearance of radiologists, have proven equally misleading. Most industrial robots perform basic tasks such as assembling, sorting and moving things around. Their rise has indeed increased the demand for specialist roles such as engineers and workers who can collaborate with robots on complex tasks. But there are few signs of a job apocalypse.

However, the bigger questions raised by the advent of robots are becoming more pressing. Machine labor has freed millions from grinding toil, enabling women, in particular, to engage in paid work. But the rise of machines often results in short-term job losses. The Luddites of the 1810s, who destroyed machines in England, were rationally responding to changes that destroyed their jobs while enriching a few. It was not until the end of that century that newly industrialized societies began to share the benefits of mechanization more fairly through clean water, sewerage, welfare states, universal education and healthcare.

Today, the debate continues on how to distribute the costs and benefits of automation more fairly. Microsoft founder Bill Gates once suggested a robot tax equivalent to the income tax of displaced workers. If jobs do shrink sharply, we might need new basic income models, an idea supported by both the political right and left. Additionally, the concentration of wealth among capital owners has prompted calls in the United States for redistributing AI-generated wealth to the wider public.

items.title: Innovation thrives on openness, cooperation: China Daily editorial
text: The 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit, held in Wuzhen, Zhejiang province, with its emphasis on open-source artificial intelligence and international cooperation, carries a timely message: technological progress is better served by openness and collaboration rather than suspicion and exclusion.

The annual gathering of the global internet community, running from Monday to Thursday, offers more than a showcase of the latest technological achievements in the sector. The development of global AI ecosystems and the governance of emerging technologies have become pressing questions for governments, businesses and societies worldwide. By bringing technology executives, researchers, developers and international representatives together for face-to-face exchanges, the Wuzhen Summit provides a valuable platform for discussing not only where AI is heading, but how its benefits and risks can be managed.

The summit's 27 sub-forums, covering almost everything from AI agents and embodied intelligence to robotics and international cyberspace governance, reflect the breadth of the opportunities and challenges. In particular, the gathering's focus on building a global open-source AI ecosystem has caught high attention. Such an ecosystem means that no country or company can determine the future of a technology that is becoming integral to the global economy. Cooperation on standards, safety and innovation is not a concession of competitive advantage; it is a prerequisite for making technological progress sustainable.

Chips, large language models and robots are increasingly interconnected components of such an ecosystem. China's innovation vitality lies precisely in this integrated chain, linking research, manufacturing and commercial applications. That is also why attempts to contain China's technological development through restrictions on individual technologies are unlikely to achieve their intended purpose.

The summit's attention to 6G is similarly forward-looking. By integrating communication, sensing, computing and AI, 6G can support intelligent transport, low-altitude aviation and connectivity across remote regions, oceans and the skies. Its significance lies in expanding the relationship between the physical and digital worlds.

The summit's discussions on one-person companies also recognize how open-source tools and AI agents are lowering the barriers to entrepreneurship. This could broaden participation in the digital economy, provided that entrepreneurial talent is given room to experiment and grow.

In addition, the summit zooms in on the prospects of the digital-intelligence consumer market, and highlights exoskeletons and brain-computer interfaces that could improve the lives of elderly people and those with disabilities.

Just as Chinese Premier Li Qiang said in a keynote speech at the opening ceremony of the Wuzhen Summit, despite rapid technological advances, one major question of common concern remains unchanged, namely how to make the internet better serve humanity.

items.title: Artist draws a nation's changing destiny
text: The career of late artist Luo Gongliu (1916-2004) reflects a lifelong artistic exploration closely intertwined with the destiny of the nation and the needs of his times. Many of his works have become iconic images in the collective memory of 20th-century China.

Exploration and Mission: An Art and Document Exhibition of Luo Gongliu, now on view at the National Museum of China in Beijing, pays homage to the artist's prolific career. It brings together works from various collections, including those of his family, the NMC and the Central Academy of Fine Arts, where he taught for decades, alongside manuscripts, photographs and other archival documents.

The exhibition traces Luo's unwavering artistic exploration, beginning with his early years as an ambitious young artist creating woodcuts. The medium was popular among socially conscious young people and was championed by prominent scholar and writer Lu Xun as a means of expressing social concerns and ideals.
Luo later trained as an oil painter, using the medium to document the country's revolutionary history and socialist construction.
In his later years, he continued to reinvent himself, drawing on the aesthetic traditions of Chinese art and producing works markedly different in style from his earlier creations.
The exhibition offers a glimpse into the journey of an artist deeply engaged with China's cultural development and the evolution of its art education.

items.title: Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019210/Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
text: A few weeks ago, I served as a judge on a food program in China, where I met many chefs and got a close look at how they develop new dishes. I was particularly impressed by one dish: a steamed egg custard topped with a rich crab paste made from crab roe and fat. It was a combination I had never considered before. The crab paste had a delicate aroma and a rich, oily texture, while the steamed egg custard was soft and silky, perfectly balancing its richness.
I was struck by the dish’s ingenuity, but it also raised a question: Would people be willing to pay for the recipe and instructions on how to make it?

I put this question to one of the chefs on the program. He smiled at me as though I were a child and asked why anyone would pay for a recipe. He then let me in on an industry secret: When a restaurant discovers that a competitor has introduced a new dish, it will order it and have its own chefs taste it, analyze its ingredients, cooking techniques, and seasonings, and work out how it was made. In most cases, they can reproduce it. The chef told me he had recreated other people’s dishes and had his own copied by others.
It all sounded rather cutthroat. The person who bears the cost of innovation often reaps little of the reward.

In Chinese cuisine, creating a new dish is not nearly as simple as diners might imagine. Chefs must find the right ingredients, adjust proportions, experiment with different cooking temperatures, refine textures, and continually adjust based on customer feedback. Developing a successful dish can involve dozens or even hundreds of failed attempts before it is ready to serve.

The time, ingredients, and labor costs of this trial-and-error process are all borne by the original creator. Yet as soon as the dish reaches the table, anyone can observe, taste, analyze, and even reproduce it. For a competitor, learning most of the techniques needed to make a dish may cost little more than the price of a meal.

Even more frustrating, many of these innovators lack the resources to promote their creations. A small restaurant might be the first to develop a dish but lack the advertising budget, media exposure, or network of locations to popularize it. Meanwhile, a larger restaurant can simply copy the dish and quickly introduce it to a wider audience. Since more people encounter it there first, they may assume the larger restaurant came up with it.

This suggests that the first-mover advantage does not necessarily apply in the restaurant business. Being first matters only if consumers know who created the dish and the original creator has the resources and business acumen to turn that innovation into a brand and a source of revenue. Otherwise, the creator is essentially providing free research and development while introducing consumers to a dish that benefits the entire market.

items.title: China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019209/China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
text: China has approved its first domestically developed amino acid-based nutritional powder, designed to give patients with phenylketonuria (PKU) — a rare genetic disorder that affects metabolism of the amino acid phenylalanine — greater freedom in what they eat. Treatment of PKU requires lifelong dietary restrictions to prevent developmental disorders and brain damage.

The new formula officially entered the Chinese market on Oct. 30 and was jointly developed by Shanghai-based Xinhua Hospital, affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research, and dairy producer Bright Dairy.
PKU affects about one in every 11,000 newborns in China, with an estimated 120,000 to 150,000 registered patients nationwide.

Due to a genetic defect, people with PKU cannot break down phenylalanine, an amino acid found in protein-rich foods. The resulting buildup can damage brain cells, requiring patients to follow a low-phenylalanine diet by cutting out meat and eating low-protein grains, while relying on milk powder-like formulas to supplement the other amino acids they need.
Earlier formulas contained 30% to 60% amino acids, with the rest composed of fats, carbohydrates, and other nutrients.

“As patients grow older, they need more protein. That means consuming more of these formulas, which also means taking in more fats and carbohydrates, increasing the risk of obesity,” Cai Wei, director of the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research and leader of the research team, told domestic media.

In contrast, the new formula contains 95% amino acids, allowing patients to meet their amino acid needs without consuming as much fat or as many carbohydrates, and giving them more freedom to enjoy other normal low-protein foods.

Zhuang Yingying, a 33-year-old PKU patient, told domestic media that patients previously relied heavily on imported products, and overseas supply disruptions were common. Special low-protein foods such as rice and noodles cost five to 10 times as much as regular varieties.
The formula, designed for PKU patients aged 1 and older, could save some families more than 1,000 yuan ($140) a month, according to domestic media.

Domestic PKU formulas have existed for decades, but long faced hurdles in gaining regulatory approval in China, partly because of gaps in national standards for food-grade amino acids, according to a 2020 report by domestic media outlet China Times. High registration costs and the small patient population have also discouraged manufacturers from entering the market.
China approved its first PKU medical formula in 2018, an imported product, while the first domestically produced formula received regulatory approval in 2025.

Since 2018, some parts of China, including Shanghai and neighboring Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces, have introduced public health insurance coverage for foods formulated for PKU patients. In Shanghai, annual coverage ranges from 8,000 yuan for infants under 1 to 12,000 yuan for patients over 10.

items.title: Inside the Chinese County Selling $2 Nails to the World
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019198/Inside the Chinese County Selling $2 Nails to the World
text: At her desk in a press-on nail workshop in Donghai, a county in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, Chai Fenfen has hung a large print of a 100-yuan banknote.
“I came here to make money,” she says. “That’s what keeps me motivated.”

After jobs selling insurance and real estate, Chai joined the workshop in 2024. Making nails offers steady earnings and the flexibility to take her children to and from school. Workers there are paid by the piece, typically earning 3,000 to 4,000 yuan a month ($450 to $600).
But for the businesses supplying that work, the early boom has given way to fierce competition over price.

Once known for its crystal trade, Donghai used its existing e-commerce networks to build an industry around press-on nails — ready-made artificial nails that customers attach themselves. By 2024, the county had nearly 25,000 businesses in the trade, according to its press-on nail industry association.
Chai’s employer, wholesaler Li Zhifu, entered the business in 2021, and now has around 2,000 workers across his production sites and more than 20 storefronts in the county.

In the beginning, Li says, almost anything sold, regardless of color or design. Competition has since squeezed profits. He estimates that six or seven out of every 10 people who entered the trade have gone out of business.
Some businesses are competing on design, selling elaborate, handmade sets for hundreds of yuan. Others are expanding overseas sales through TikTok Shop.
As overseas orders grow, Li is experimenting with machines to make nails his workers currently produce by hand.
“For large overseas orders, consistency is key. Everything, from colors and designs to rhinestone placement, has to match,” he says. He expects machine-made nails to eventually dominate that market.
(Header image: Craftswomen work in a press-on nail workshop in Donghai County, Jiangsu province, August 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

items.title: China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019203/China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
text: China’s latest viral reality show is about broken friendships — rather than failing romance — between celebrities.

“I Miss You” surpassed 100 million views within two days of its Oct. 22 debut, and topped the real-time TV popularity chart on Chinese review platform Douban since last Thursday. Topics related to the show have repeatedly trended on the microblogging platform Weibo since airing.
Produced by streaming platform Mango TV, the show brings together four pairs of celebrities who have reportedly fallen out for an 18-day trip through the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region.

The show is widely seen as a riff on China’s popular relationship reality shows and follows a similar format to “See You Again,” whose fifth season aired in late 2025, which takes celebrity couples in troubled marriages on an 18-day trip before they decide whether to divorce.

In “I Miss You,” guests discuss their former friendships as a group and one-on-one with their ex-friends, play games, and share their feelings with the production team. A panel of celebrities, a psychologist, and a journalist comment on their interactions.

The most discussed pair on “I Miss You” so far has been Xu Fei and Li Na, two contestants from the 2006 season of “Super Girl,” a popular televised singing competition regarded as a cornerstone of China’s fan culture.

The two were close friends during the competition 20 years ago, but their friendship later collapsed after Li came to believe that Xu had reported her to their management company for taking outside jobs in violation of her contract. Li said the company subsequently stopped arranging work for her, which she sees as having dealt a major blow to her career. Xu denied the accusation, instead blaming a third person.
As the two revisited their past on the show, their memories of their friendship moved many viewers, with one highly upvoted comment describing their relationship as “an epic saga of love and hate.”

Xu said in tears that she had loved “wasting time together,” and noted that her current preferred snacks are the “ones Li loved back then.” Li also recalled how, even when the two appeared to be bitter enemies, they would sometimes end up crying in each other’s arms after getting drunk at gatherings.
Yet the two remained at odds over the past accusation. During an interview with the production team, Li said she had hated Xu “for a long time,” at one point shouting, “What about the money I lost?”

The other three pairs of celebrities include an actor who cut ties with a longtime producer friend after feeling pressured to accept a role, an actress and a writer who fell out when the latter grew closer to a third person, and former professional esports teammates who fought over training strategies, eventually leading one to leave the team.

“‘I Miss You’ feels so much more pure than ‘See You Again,’” read a post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, that received almost 3,700 likes. “In a marriage, you have to argue about more than feelings. There’s property, children, parents, and so much else. With friendship, we can sit down and focus on just one thing: how we feel about each other.”

items.title: Writing on the Wall? How AI Is Reinventing Chinese Typography
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019200/Writing on the Wall? How AI Is Reinventing Chinese Typography
text: Many assume the writing is on the wall for human typographers. For decades, the industry has been slowly decimated by the advance of digital publishing software. Now, artificial intelligence is here to finish off the job.

That view has only strengthened since the launch of OpenAI’s Image 2.0 earlier this year. Until then, type designers and typographers had clung to the hope that AI would never be able to replace them: AI-generated fonts and layouts had always looked clunky, inconsistent, error-ridden, or somehow just a bit off.

But Image 2.0’s capabilities took many by surprise: it was able to produce beautifully designed documents featuring long passages of text in multiple languages, while maintaining a high degree of accuracy. The work was not as good as that produced by professional type designers, but for a layperson looking to make a poster or a brochure, it was just fine.

Suddenly, typography — perhaps the last stronghold of graphic design still firmly controlled by professional designers — looked at risk of falling as well. If everyone can generate typefaces and layouts with a simple prompt, or even ask a frontier AI model to operate design software on its own — just as non-programmers can now “write code” through vibe coding — how many designers will lose their jobs?

In the English-speaking world, the AI revolution may indeed prove to be a hammer blow for the typography community. But things are likely to play out a little differently in China: the relationship between text and technology has always been more complex due to the nature of its writing system.

Most contemporary typographic practice derives from movable-type printing technology. Developed in medieval Germany, typography is closely tied to the inherent characteristics of the Latin alphabet: there are only a few dozen letters, and the same letters recur constantly throughout a printed text.

With these characteristics in mind, Johannes Gutenberg developed an entire technological process of carving, reproducing, retrieving, and repeatedly reusing individual letter forms. Once a complete set of letters had been produced, it could be used to print texts containing vast numbers of repetitions of exactly the same glyphs.

Gutenberg would later be credited as a pioneer of movable type printing, a technology whose logic has been carried intact from books to the screen you are now looking at. But applying this technique to Chinese characters is a huge challenge, as there is such a vast number of them. While function words such as de may appear repeatedly on a single page, most characters may occur only once or twice in a given text — or not at all.

Statistically, 3,500 characters is enough to cover most everyday text — studies have shown they account for 99.5% of character usage. But to avoid the awkward situation where a character outside the “common 3,500” can’t be rendered properly, the industry often sets 7,000 characters as the target size for a typeface. Some larger projects cover 27,000, or even 87,000 characters.

Why a Guangdong state giant’s troubles are rippling across China’s bond market
text: Mounting concerns over Huafa’s finances have shaken China’s bond market and renewed scrutiny of local governments’ reliance on land sales

At the centre of the storm is Zhuhai Huafa Group, the largest local government-owned enterprise in Zhuhai in southern China’s Guangdong province. While property development remains its core business, the conglomerate also has interests spanning technology, urban operations and financial services.

With more than 93 per cent of its equity owned by Zhuhai’s State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission and the remainder held by Guangdong’s finance department, Huafa was deeply intertwined with the city’s development, including projects such as the Hengqin New Area, analysts said.

      Hong Kong — 
    

    
            A former elementary school teacher has been propelled into the ranks of paper billionaires in China after the stock debut of his company selling tape and other adhesive products to tech giants, according to Forbes.

Michael Mai, chairman and CEO of Crown New Materials Technology, entered the rarefied financial heights on Tuesday when the company, which produces binding agents for major brands like Tesla and Apple, made its trading debut on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange.

Shares shot up as much as 787%, from 16.98 yuan ($2.55) per share in its stock filing to a height of 150.58 yuan ($22.57) per share at one point, according to the Shenzhen bourse, mainland China’s second-largest stock exchange.
Mai, an Australian citizen and permanent resident of Hong Kong, has an estimated net worth of $2.5 billion, based on his stake in the firm, Forbes reported.
The 62-year-old was reportedly an elementary school teacher in the southern Chinese city of Zhongshan – where the company, founded in 2000, is based.
His sister, Mai Huixia, 64, who serves as vice-chairperson, joined him in the billionaire ranks, with Forbes reporting that her stake gave her a $2 billion fortune.
Shares eased to about 77 yuan ($12) per share Wednesday morning following the peak a day earlier that prompted the company to call on investors in a statement to “invest rationally.”
CNN has reached out to the company for comment.

Weapon or wine bottle? China disputes reports of artillery shell in Papua New Guinea
text: Chinese authorities have dismissed reports that a suspected China-made artillery shell was found in a commercial shipping container in Papua New Guinea, saying it is a "shell-shaped wine bottle".
"It poses no danger at all," the Chinese embassy wrote in a Facebook post on Tuesday, drawing sceptical comments.
Police in Port Moresby arrested four Chinese nationals last Friday after the 32kg object was found at a construction site in the capital city.
Authorities were looking into whether it was a live device, local reports said then, with police commissioner David Manning describing it as "a very concerning discovery".

In a report on Wednesday, the Australia Broadcasting Corporation cited unnamed sources identifying the object as an undetonated 130mm Chinese Type 59 Artillery Projectile that contains chemical explosives and a fuse. The BBC has not independently verified this.
Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that the object was "merely a dummy", local newspaper Post Courier said.
However, the Chinese embassy said in its statement that it is "virtually impossible" for an illegal military-grade artillery shell to be smuggled out of China to Papua New Guinea.
"China enforces some of the world's strictest firearm control laws and regulations," it wrote, adding that China is "widely recognised as one of the safest countries globally".
"What sort of wine bottle weighs 32 kilograms?" wrote one of them.
Another wrote that the object bore no labels indicating that it's a wine bottle.

How are parts of Tibet’s ground ice thickening despite rapid warming?
text: Research counters expectations but the region remains extremely vulnerable to climate change, study warns

A team from Peking University found that shallow ground ice has unexpectedly increased over the past 20 years, affecting more than a third of the plateau’s permafrost, a phenomenon driven largely by natural climate factors.
The authors noted that the impact of this ice gain on the stability of the underlying permafrost and the broader environment was unclear.
